section_summary: This section documents the State Department’s effort to obtain custody of, or at least unrestricted access to, Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and official property after Japan’s surrender. Embassies across Europe, Latin America, and Asia report negotiations with protecting powers and local governments, while Washington coordinates policy with Britain, China, the Soviet Union, and General MacArthur’s headquarters. The papers also include evidence from seized archives concerning Japanese intelligence activity and financial assets, notably records from Brazil, Panama, Peru, Chile, and Mexico.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 1230: No Action Required in Paraguay Regarding Japanese Government Archives and Property
subfiles.from: Willard L. Beaulac, U.S. Embassy, Asunción
subfiles.about: Reports that no further action is necessary because Paraguay holds no Japanese diplomatic or consular archives or property.
subfiles.summary: The Paraguayan Ministry of Foreign Relations states that no Japanese diplomatic or consular archives or official property exist in Paraguay. Beaulac therefore recommends closing the matter locally.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1365 from Santiago on custody arrangements
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Seeks clarification on whether Japanese archives should go to the three represented Allied powers or to the Chilean government.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy notes that no Soviet representative is present and that British instructions permit Chile to receive the archives if it wishes. The American, British, and Chinese missions agree to await instructions to the Swedish minister before acting.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 3682 from Moscow requesting authority to transmit the directive
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, U.S. Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Asks whether General MacArthur’s directive concerning Japanese archives may be communicated to the Soviet government.
subfiles.summary: Harriman requests an immediate ruling on whether any reason exists not to give the directive to Soviet authorities. The telegram is marked urgent and secret.

subfiles.title: Department telegram no. 5321 to Paris on joint access
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs that access to Japanese property and archives be requested jointly by the four Allied representatives.
subfiles.summary: The Department authorizes French reciprocal inspection after custody has been obtained. It rejects delaying action until a Soviet expert arrives and requests information on methods for obtaining prompt inspection.

subfiles.title: Department telegram approving the proposed Hague procedure
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Approves the procedure proposed in Hague telegram no. 139 and requests a report on the examination method.
subfiles.summary: Washington accepts the proposed joint approach to the Netherlands government. The Embassy is asked to explain how examination of the archives will be conducted.

subfiles.title: Department telegram authorizing communication to the Soviet government
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.about: Authorizes the Embassy to communicate and quote the archives directive to the Soviet government.
subfiles.summary: The Department answers Harriman’s request affirmatively. The full text of the directive may be quoted to Soviet authorities.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 638 from Managua
subfiles.from: Avra M. Warren, U.S. Embassy, Managua
subfiles.about: Reports that no Japanese diplomatic or consular mission existed in Nicaragua.
subfiles.summary: Warren refers to the Department’s October 23 circular and an earlier Embassy telegram. Because Japan maintained no mission in Nicaragua, there are no mission archives to secure.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 139 from The Hague proposing a joint note
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, U.S. Embassy, The Hague
subfiles.about: Submits a proposed four-power note requesting access to Japanese archives held by the Netherlands.
subfiles.summary: The British, American, Chinese, and Soviet ambassadors agree on a draft request to the Netherlands foreign minister. The note asks that their governments share the right to examine Japanese diplomatic and consular archives, while a proposed reference to the Netherlands West Indies is deleted.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 6260 from Paris on French access and reciprocity
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, U.S. Embassy, Paris
subfiles.about: Requests instructions on access, possible French reciprocity, and the proposed delay for a Soviet Japanese-language expert.
subfiles.summary: The four Allied missions have received no instructions and fear that transfer to France may omit their right of access. They anticipate a French demand for reciprocal rights and note that none has a Japanese reader, prompting the Soviet representative to favor delay until an expert arrives.

subfiles.title: Wadsworth memorandum on Japanese and German consular archives in Beirut
subfiles.from: George Wadsworth
subfiles.about: Explains the seizure of Japanese archives in Beirut and recommends raising the French handling of German archives.
subfiles.summary: Wadsworth says he acted under Department instructions with British and Soviet concurrence and notified French and Lebanese authorities as a courtesy. He recommends telling France that the Japanese action followed Allied policy while asking whether French officials in Beirut will make German archives available to the four powers victorious over Germany.

subfiles.title: Hague despatch proposing alternative language for the Netherlands request
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, U.S. Embassy, The Hague
subfiles.about: Forwards alternative draft language for seeking access to Japanese archives in Netherlands custody.
subfiles.summary: The badly reproduced despatch follows the four-ambassador meeting and discusses whether the Netherlands should be asked about archives already or later coming into its hands. It presents alternative formulations centered on sharing access with American, British, Chinese, and Soviet representatives.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1089 from Lima on missing Swedish instructions
subfiles.from: William D. Pawley, U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Reports that the Swedish chargé has not received authority from Stockholm to surrender Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The Swedish chargé remains without instructions despite the Department’s October 23 circular. The Embassy therefore cannot yet complete the proposed transfer.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3341: Japanese Archives and Japanese Intelligence Activities
subfiles.from: Adolf A. Berle Jr., U.S. Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Forwards a Legal Attaché memorandum on Suetaka Hayao and reports the status of Japanese archives in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The Swedish Legation has not yet received instructions to surrender the Japanese archives, and Brazil is still expected to take custody. Berle anticipates arranging a cooperative examination with the Brazilian Foreign Ministry once the transfer occurs.

subfiles.title: Legal Attaché memorandum concerning Suetaka Hayao
subfiles.from: Heber M. Clegg, Legal Attaché
subfiles.to: U.S. Ambassador in Brazil, attention Mr. Daniels
subfiles.about: Reports interviews with former Japanese diplomat Suetaka Hayao about espionage, a coded message, and Embassy files.
subfiles.summary: Hayao denies participating in organized Japanese espionage and claims he cannot decode a suspect message transmitted from Buenos Aires through Nipo-Brasileira. The Legal Attaché plans to question Ryokichi Nagai and observes that Hayao appears worried about American examination of Japanese Embassy files.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Japanese archives policy
subfiles.from: G. R. Ranken, British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.to: A. E. Clattenburg Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains Britain’s position that access should be sought but pressure for physical custody should be avoided.
subfiles.summary: Britain supports transfer of Japanese official property and archives to representatives of the Four Powers. It nevertheless considers the records too unimportant to justify pressuring an objecting belligerent government and instructs its missions to settle for permission to examine them.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on revising the archives procedure
subfiles.from: Mr. Williams, Special War Problems Division
subfiles.about: Records agreement to replace “direction” with “agreement” in instructions concerning Japanese property and archives.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Gross argues that China, Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union can no longer claim exclusive authority to direct SCAP. Williams and Lory concur, and the amended paper is to be forwarded to Mr. Russell.

subfiles.title: Ballantine memorandum on pending policy questions
subfiles.from: J. W. Ballantine, Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Advises suspending field action until General MacArthur issues orders and notes uncertainty over Japan’s future foreign representation.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine sees no practical alternative to holding the archives question in abeyance and suggests telling missions to desist temporarily. He also notes that custody policy depends on whether Japanese diplomatic representation abroad will be abolished or merely reduced.

subfiles.title: Straus memorandum: History and problems of Japanese diplomatic archives policy
subfiles.from: O. S. Straus, Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: Summarizes the origin of the archives campaign and poses unresolved questions about delay and future Japanese representation.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces instructions issued from August 14 through approaches to Bern and General MacArthur after Japan rejected the demand as outside the Potsdam Declaration. It asks what missions should do during a potentially lengthy delay and whether custody should be permanent or temporary if Japanese missions are eventually allowed to continue.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 27,048: Disposition of Japanese Diplomatic and Consular Archives in Mexico
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports four-power consultations over whether Japanese archives in Mexico should pass to Allied representatives or the Mexican government.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith expects Mexico to demand custody while granting the Allies full access, following its handling of German archives. He describes British and Chinese cooperation, criticizes the Soviet chargé’s guarded and distrustful posture, and awaits the Swedish minister’s instructions before reconvening the group.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the files on Naval Intelligence access
subfiles.from: P. F. Cherp, Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: Records Lieutenant Commander Robinson’s request for information and naval access to Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Robinson is assured that the Navy Department and naval attachés will be permitted access. Field examination is expected to be conducted by mixed mission, legal, military, and naval teams, and Robinson asks to be notified when Tokyo implements the directive.

subfiles.title: Department telegram no. 1779 to Chongqing
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to keep the Chinese Foreign Office informed about the Japanese archives and property program.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy may communicate the text and substance of the Department’s October 23 and October 25 circulars. The instruction responds to Chongqing telegram no. 1901.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-51 to Panama requesting the original Japanese text
subfiles.from: Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests a photostatic copy so that a new translation can determine how Japanese mission funds were disposed of.
subfiles.summary: Washington concludes that funds were probably removed through action by the former Japanese minister and staff. It notes that custody accounts were common in Japanese missions and orders investigation of whether the money was governmental or privately owned.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1901 from Chongqing
subfiles.from: Walter S. Robertson, U.S. Embassy, Chongqing
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Department’s recent archives circulars may be shared with the Chinese Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese Foreign Office has requested information about Japanese archives and property in belligerent and neutral countries. The Embassy seeks permission to convey the substance of the October 23 and October 25 instructions.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3147: Analysis of used carbon paper found in Japanese Legation archives
subfiles.from: Walter J. Donnelly, U.S. Embassy, Panama
subfiles.about: Reports FBI analysis indicating that Japanese Legation officers removed $33,900 or $39,900 from Panama.
subfiles.summary: Seven recovered carbon sheets concern deposits associated with the Yokohama Specie Bank that were divided among five Japanese officials for carriage to Japan. Donnelly suggests the funds came from residents of Panama and asks whether Minister Akiyama and his staff violated financial regulations under cover of diplomatic immunity.

subfiles.title: FBI Laboratory report and translations of recovered Japanese carbon papers
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Legal Attaché, U.S. Embassy, Panama City
subfiles.about: Presents photographic examination and translations of thirteen used carbon sheets from the Japanese Legation in Panama.
subfiles.summary: The principal translations document funds allocated to Akiyama, Izawa, Hara, Nishikawa, and Arai, with additional depositor names and amounts. Other sheets preserve routine shipping and diplomatic correspondence concerning Japanese personnel, ministers, families, official supplies, travel through Panama and Costa Rica, and visitors bound for Colombia.

subfiles.title: Department distribution memorandum forwarding the Panama carbon-paper report
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the Panama despatch on Japanese Legation carbon papers and removed funds to intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards the information in the hope that it will be useful. The enclosure is the Embassy report concerning the removal of $33,900 or $39,900 from Panama.

subfiles.title: Messersmith covering letter forwarding despatch no. 27,048
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith
subfiles.about: Forwards the Mexico archives despatch and draws attention to the Soviet representative’s conception of collaboration.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith describes the enclosed despatch as self-explanatory but particularly revealing of his Soviet colleague’s conduct. He sends it personally to Carrigan alongside the formal Department submission.

subfiles.title: Enclosed copy of despatch no. 27,048 on archives in Mexico
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the report on negotiations over Japanese diplomatic and consular archives in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The despatch anticipates Mexican custody combined with direct Allied access and waits for instructions to the Swedish minister. Messersmith emphasizes British and Chinese cooperation while portraying the Soviet chargé as evasive and suspicious of Mexico.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 329 from Tangier on archives in Casablanca
subfiles.from: Paul H. Alling, U.S. Legation, Tangier
subfiles.about: Reports arrangements for requesting access to Japanese archives and property in Casablanca.
subfiles.summary: During a visit to Madrid, Alling arranged for the Embassy to ask Spain to instruct its consul in Casablanca. The property and archives would be made available to American, British, and French representatives there.

subfiles.title: Damaged telegram on local transfer arrangements
subfiles.from: Unidentified U.S. diplomatic mission
subfiles.about: Discusses a protecting power and local arrangements for control of Japanese archives under the Department’s circular instructions.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR is severely damaged but refers to the Department’s circular, a Swiss role, a local government, and consultation with three Allied powers. It appears to concern whether Japanese archives should be placed in local custody or under representatives of the Four Powers.

subfiles.title: Messersmith letter to Carrigan on implementing the Mexico policy
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith
subfiles.about: Thanks Carrigan for policy guidance and explains how the newly granted flexibility should resolve the Mexico archives question.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith believes Mexico can take custody so long as Allied access is protected and says Geist can handle the issue during his absence. He adds that the Japanese apparently destroyed everything of significance before leaving Mexico.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 2205 from Lisbon on implementation of the directive
subfiles.from: Herman B. Baruch, U.S. Embassy, Lisbon
subfiles.about: Asks whether Tokyo actually transmitted the MacArthur directive to Japanese missions in neutral countries.
subfiles.summary: Reliable information indicates that the Japanese mission in Lisbon had received no instructions at the beginning of the week. The Embassy also cites a radio report that Japan requested modification of the directive and seeks confirmation from Washington.

subfiles.title: Circular telegram on accepting access in place of custody
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.to: American diplomatic missions, with listed exceptions
subfiles.about: Authorizes missions to accept assured access instead of physical custody where foreign offices seriously object.
subfiles.summary: The circular explains that Britain will not press belligerent governments for custody because it considers the archives of limited importance. American missions may adopt the same position with Chinese and Soviet concurrence, although they should not initiate such a concession.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 3357 from Stockholm reporting Japan’s compliance instructions
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, U.S. Legation, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese government’s surrender instructions and the sealing of its Legation in Stockholm.
subfiles.summary: Japan orders Sweden to deliver Japanese archives and property in protected countries and directs its own mission in Sweden to surrender its holdings and return home. Swedish, British, Soviet, and American representatives seal the Legation, secure a box containing 520,000 kronor, and establish an inter-Allied inspection committee, although most important records are believed destroyed.

subfiles.title: Department telegram no. 2024 requesting details from Stockholm
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests prompt information on Japanese and Swedish instructions concerning the records and property transfer.
subfiles.summary: The Legation is asked when Sweden received Japan’s message, when Sweden issued implementing instructions, and what those instructions required. A repeat is requested for Bern.

subfiles.title: Department telegram to SCAP requesting notice of implementation
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.to: George Atcheson Jr., Acting Political Adviser, SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests immediate notice when Japan implements MacArthur’s directive on overseas archives and property.
subfiles.summary: Washington seeks direct confirmation that the Japanese government has acted. The request covers both diplomatic and consular archives and official property.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 722 from Havana on retaining ministry custody
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Recommends leaving minor Japanese archives and property with the Cuban Ministry of State unless it expressly requests an American takeover.
subfiles.summary: Access to the small archive is already freely granted, while the remaining assets are mostly furniture and a small cash sum. British, Soviet, and Chinese representatives do not object to continued ministry custody.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 88 from Tokyo confirming overseas instructions
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Tokyo
subfiles.about: Confirms that Japan issued telegraphic instructions to its missions abroad on October 31.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson reports learning that day that the Japanese government had acted. The message answers Washington’s request for confirmation of implementation.

subfiles.title: Foreign Activity Correlation memorandum on the British archives aide-mémoire
subfiles.from: P. F. Cherp, Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: Comments skeptically on Britain’s request for equal examination of records under U.S. military control in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum calls the British concern belated and says it raises wider questions about archives in China and the Pacific. It assumes U.S. Army authorities preserved the records and recommends leaving the aide-mémoire pending without acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 976 from Panama recommending return of archives
subfiles.from: Frank T. Hines, U.S. Embassy, Panama
subfiles.about: Recommends returning examined archives to Panama and relinquishing claims to Japanese physical property.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy and British and Chinese ministers have had access to the records since September and have reported their findings. They propose returning the archives with a continuing right of access and leaving furniture, automobiles, and household equipment to the Panamanian government.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1117 from Lima on moving property and surrendering funds
subfiles.from: Trueblood, U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Requests guidance while preparing to take physical custody of Japanese furniture, safes, papers, and substantial currency holdings.
subfiles.summary: At Chinese insistence, the Embassy plans to move stored property into its residence so the Swedish chargé can report completion of the transfer. Trueblood asks whether Washington should send a safe expert and whether $145,000 and approximately 250,000 soles should also be surrendered to the three powers.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1114 from Lima reporting receipt of safes and papers
subfiles.from: Trueblood, U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Reports the initial transfer of four safes and three boxes of Japanese papers from the Swedish chargé.
subfiles.summary: The transfer follows arrangements made with British and Chinese representatives under Ambassador Pawley’s instructions. Most material is stored in the Embassy office, while an oversized safe is placed in a locked garage pending decisions on the remaining property.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 171 from The Hague requesting a prompt decision
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, U.S. Embassy, The Hague
subfiles.about: Reports British and Soviet approval of the proposed Netherlands note and asks for Washington’s decision.
subfiles.summary: The British ambassador states that both London and Moscow agree entirely with the note and procedure proposed in telegram no. 139. Hornbeck says an early indication of the Department’s wishes would be helpful.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1120 from Lima on currency surrender
subfiles.from: Trueblood, U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Reports that the Swedish chargé will surrender a U.S.-currency fund while seeking instructions about a soles-denominated fund.
subfiles.summary: The Swedish chargé informs the Peruvian Foreign Office that the archives and property are being transferred and agrees to give the three powers the dollar fund previously discussed. He intends not to disclose that fund to Peru, resists surrendering the soles fund without Stockholm’s approval, and asks for Washington’s views.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1256 from Athens
subfiles.from: Lincoln MacVeagh, U.S. Embassy, Athens
subfiles.about: Reports that archives circulars need not be sent to Athens because Japan withdrew its mission in 1936.
subfiles.summary: The Greek Foreign Office says no Japanese archives or protecting power remain in Greece. The Embassy therefore regards further instructions as unnecessary.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1357 from Bogotá requesting deferred action
subfiles.from: John C. Wiley, U.S. Embassy, Bogotá
subfiles.about: Suggests postponing action on Japanese archives in Colombia until Wiley can consult personally in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Wiley expects to reach Washington on November 19. Because no local pressure requires immediate action, he asks that the disposition question be deferred.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1401 from Santiago reporting transfer of archives and funds
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Reports formal receipt of Japanese archives, cash, and bonds from the Swedish minister in Chile.
subfiles.summary: With no objection from Chile, Bowers takes custody for the American, British, and Chinese representatives in the presence of a Chilean official. The records include a minister’s diary, a list of Japanese subjects, and reports on American war industries; the transfer also yields three million pesos in bonds and 900,000 pesos in cash, for which instructions are requested.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 219 from Vatican City
subfiles.from: Harold H. Tittmann Jr., Vatican City
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese ambassador to the Holy See has received no implementing instructions from Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Montini says the ambassador earlier received only an informational summary of MacArthur’s directive and Japan’s objection that it conflicted with the Potsdam Declaration. Ambassador Harada nevertheless states that he is prepared to comply as soon as orders arrive.

subfiles.title: Turner memorandum on the applicability of the recall directive to the Vatican
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Japanese Affairs
subfiles.to: P. F. Cherp, Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: Explains that the Vatican telegram was withheld until the War Department clarified the Japanese representative’s status.
subfiles.summary: The War Department has informed MacArthur that his October 25 recall directive applies to the Japanese representative at the Vatican. Turner recommends telling Tittmann that Tokyo’s instructions should follow soon and requesting another report if no action becomes apparent.

subfiles.title: Unsent telegram to SCAP concerning the Japanese ambassador at the Vatican
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.to: George Atcheson Jr., Acting Political Adviser, SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Drafts a request for action because the Japanese ambassador at the Vatican had not received instructions about records and property.
subfiles.summary: The draft asks SCAP to take appropriate action and report. It was explicitly marked not sent, pending clarification of relations between the Japanese government and the Vatican.

subfiles.title: Background memorandum for Braden on Japanese records and archives policy
subfiles.from: Foreign Activity Correlation Division
subfiles.about: Summarizes the evolution and current status of U.S. policy on Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces the campaign from the August 14 instructions through Japan’s initial rejection, MacArthur’s October directive, and the local-discretion circulars. It explains British preference for access over custody, notes difficulties particularly in South America, and concludes that full access and photographic reproduction matter more than who ultimately preserves the records.
